as_told: Scientists put five monkeys in a cage with a banana at the top of a ladder. Whenever a monkey climbed toward it, all the monkeys were sprayed with cold water, so they learned to beat any monkey that tried. The monkeys were then replaced one at a time, until none had ever been sprayed, yet they still beat any monkey that climbed the ladder. Nobody knew why; that was just how things were done.
lesson: Groups keep enforcing rules long after the reason for them is gone, and newcomers learn the rule without the reason.
what_happened: No experiment matching the story was found. The earliest telling found, Hamel and Prahalad, Competing for the Future (1994), credits 'a friend of ours' and gives no source; it has four monkeys and a pole. Later retellings name a 1967 study by Gordon R. Stephenson. Stephenson's own description (1968 congress paper, published 1969) shows a different study: monkeys in pairs, one monkey punished with an air blast when it touched a plastic kitchen object. Sometimes the naive partner then avoided the object, and once the trained monkey pulled the naive one away by the hind legs. In other pairs the trained monkey lost its fear after watching the naive one handle the object. There were no five monkeys, no ladder, no banana, no water spray and no chain of replacements.
false_part: The study that retellers name as the experiment (Stephenson 1967) did happen and did show that monkeys can pass on the avoidance of an object to a naive partner. But the details that the lesson needs are false: there was no group of five, no replacement of the monkeys one by one, and no finding that the rule outlived every trained monkey. In some pairs the fear passed the other way, from the naive monkey to the trained one, and it faded. The ladder, banana and cold-water spray are also not in the study.

lesson_verdict.why: Laboratory studies of arbitrary traditions, where members are replaced one at a time, find that a tradition persists for some replacements and then fades toward what is useful. That supports a partial and temporary version of the lesson, not the strong claim that a rule lasts unchanged after everyone who knew its reason is gone.

confidence_note: Stephenson's 1967 chapter itself was not read; his 1969 summary was read only as Open Library snippets, pieced together. The friend Hamel and Prahalad mention is not named, so a private source for the story cannot be ruled out, but no experiment like it was found. The class is changed and not invented because the record that retellers point to (Stephenson) exists and shows a related but different event; the earliest telling found (1994) does not itself cite Stephenson, so if that link is rejected, the class would be unsupported.
